title: Poland's Orka Submarine Program Turns Industrial While Japan Reopens the Nuclear-Propulsion Question
subhead: Navantia launched Saudi Arabia's seventh Avante corvette in Cádiz, Saab locked in French propulsion and Swedish training boats for Poland's A26 fleet, and Tokyo's defense minister kept nuclear-powered submarines formally on the table. Baltic and Northeast Asian undersea recapitalization is now a supply-chain story, not a strategy paper.

sections.heading: Poland's Orka Program Moves From Contract to Supply Chain
sections.body:
Two industrial announcements in 48 hours show how far Poland's Orka submarine program has moved past the signature stage. French electrical manufacturer Jeumont Electric has secured a contract with Saab to supply three complete electric propulsion systems for the Polish Navy's A26 (Blekinge-class) boats, Naval News reported. Jeumont already equips Sweden's own Blekinge-class and the Saab-designed Collins-class for Australia, and the company emphasized that its drives are recognized for low acoustic signature — the decisive variable in the shallow, confined Baltic.

Separately, Sweden's FMV and the Swedish Navy signed formal implementation contracts covering Polish crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland. Training for the first Polish crews is already running in Karlskrona with the 1st Submarine Flotilla and the Naval Warfare Centre; the course lasts 18 months, the same length as a Swedish crew's. The leased Södermanland, a modernized Västergötland-class boat with Stirling air-independent propulsion, gives Warsaw hands-on AIP experience ahead of first A26 deliveries scheduled for 2031.
sections.whyItMatters: Poland is buying a submarine capability as a package — hulls, propulsion, training, weapons, and an interim boat — rather than a hull with a promise attached. That is the difference between a program that delivers a working crew in 2031 and one that delivers three submarines and no trained operators. It also quietly deepens a Paris-Stockholm-Warsaw undersea chain that runs independently of German and US suppliers.

sections.heading: Japan Keeps Nuclear Propulsion on the Table as Seoul Moves First
sections.body:
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has confirmed that Tokyo is not ruling out nuclear-powered submarines as it reviews the country's key security documents, according to reporting by The War Zone and Naval News. Japan currently operates 22 conventionally powered submarines built around the Taigei class, widely regarded as among the most capable diesel-electric forces afloat, with air-independent propulsion and advanced lithium-ion batteries.

No decision and no procurement program exist. But the debate itself matters: nuclear propulsion would give the JMSDF sustained underwater speed and endurance for long-range Western Pacific surveillance and sea-denial missions that conventional boats cannot sustain. The shift is regional, not isolated — Seoul has confirmed plans for its own nuclear-powered submarine class (the Jang Bogo N Project), and Australia is acquiring nuclear boats under AUKUS Pillar I. TWZ notes that a Japanese SSN decision could eventually open deeper interoperability with Australia on undersea warfare, workforce and infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan moving from 'unthinkable' to 'not ruled out' is a change in what Tokyo's defense establishment is willing to plan around, driven by the same problem Seoul and Canberra are answering. The practical constraint is not political will but infrastructure — reactor design, fuel cycle, and regulatory machinery Japan does not currently have, all of which would take a decade or more to stand up.

sections.heading: Navantia Launches Saudi Corvette 'Neom' on a Four-Month Drumbeat
sections.body:
On October 25, Navantia launched the seventh Avante 2200 corvette for the Royal Saudi Naval Forces at its Bay of Cádiz shipyards. The ship, to be named HMS Neom, is the second of a three-ship batch contracted in 2025, following five built between 2019 and 2024. Navantia Chairman Ricardo Domínguez said the yard is now launching one ship every four months, describing it as in line with the program's industrial schedule.

The corvettes carry Navantia's own HAZEM combat system (via the SAMINavantia joint venture), HERMESYS communications, DORNA fire control, and MTU-licensed propulsion. The program is worth roughly four million working hours to the Cádiz region, averaging 2,200 skilled jobs per day, with more than 20 subcontractors and 50 suppliers. Two of the three ships in this batch will be sent to Saudi Arabia for combat-system installation and testing, as happened with hulls four and five.
sections.whyItMatters: The interesting number is the drumbeat, not the hull. A yard holding a four-month launch cadence on a repeat design is a different industrial animal from one that delivers a ship and then reconstitutes a team. Spanish yards are becoming the reliable second-tier European producer for Gulf navies while the largest European programs absorb capacity elsewhere.

sections.heading: AUTOWARCOM Has a Mission and a Command Structure — What It Lacks Is Money and People
sections.body:
Defense One reports that funding and force structure could hinder Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's new US Autonomous Warfare Command. The $54 billion for the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group is to come from a reconciliation bill whose passage is far from assured, even among Republicans allied with the administration, with midterms approaching.

The structural problem is that AUTOWARCOM is modelled on functional combatant commands like Cyber Command and Special Operations Command, but is being built in reverse: the plan calls for creating service component commands where none existed and a new autonomous-warfare corps of officers and enlisted personnel, and neither Hegseth's directive nor the more recent implementation guidance explains how those specialties integrate with existing units. Mark Cancian of CSIS told Defense One that a four-star command whose primary mission is acquisition 'doesn't make a whole lot of sense,' arguing a Missile Defense Agency-style three-star command with its own budget would fit better — and that letting one centralized command take over drone operations across the services would be a bad idea. Retired general John G. Ferrari of AEI was blunter on the timeline: 'Either the money shows up by Christmas or it ain't coming, because when the new Congress gets seated in January, there is no reconciliation anymore.' A plan of action and milestones is due at the end of this month.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is standing up an acquisition command before it has secured the appropriation that justifies it — the same sequencing that produced the F-35 and KC-46 pattern of a program office outrunning its funding line. If the reconciliation money does not arrive by the new Congress, AUTOWARCOM becomes an organization with a charter and no buying power, and the services absorb the drone budget fight instead.

sections.heading: The Interceptor Race Turns to Jet-Powered Shaheds
sections.body:
US dronemaker Powerus is targeting rocket- or jet-powered interceptors as its next product, Defense One reported, after a surge in Russia's use of jet-powered Shahed drones in Ukraine. Company president Brett Velicovich said the goal is an interceptor flying at 600-700 km/h, which he argued will require substantially more automation and R&D. He expects that by the end of this year the majority of Russian drones sent into downtown Kyiv could be jet-powered.

The economics are the constraint: Velicovich said Russia builds the upgraded Shaheds for $20,000-$30,000 in massive quantities, a price point an interceptor has to approach. Powerus unveiled the fully autonomous Guardian 3 at AUSA, aims for 5,000 interceptors per month by November with an eventual goal of ten times that, and signed a deal with Parsons to pair its radars with Guardian interceptors. Separately at AUSA, US-Norwegian startup Heaviside launched the Tyr anti-tank loitering munition — roughly 15 pounds, a third of it warhead sourced from Norway's Nammo, priced 'way under $100,000,' with EO/IR-fused video navigation that lets the drone find a tank autonomously and ask an operator for permission to strike.
sections.whyItMatters: Counter-drone procurement is splitting into two markets: cheap interceptors that must be built like artillery rounds, and autonomous munitions cheap enough to expend on a single vehicle. Both are being shaped by a price ceiling set by Russian and Iranian production, not by Western cost-plus accounting — and companies are designing to that ceiling rather than to a requirement document.

sections.heading: Space Force Makes Its First Real Commercial Reserve Buys — $1.37 Million Worth
sections.body:
Space Systems Command awarded the first 'operational' contracts under the Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative to six space-monitoring firms: Australia's EOS Space Systems, Canada's NorthStar Earth and Space, InTrack Radar, Anduril (via its ExoAnalytic acquisition), Slingshot Aerospace, and LeoLabs. The total value is $1.37 million across short-term contracts, an SSC spokesperson told Breaking Defense. The awards follow $1.1 million in three-month pilot contracts to four unnamed companies in March 2025.

Two unresolved issues remain before the model can scale, per Breaking Defense: whether Washington gets the right to shut off a CASR partner's services to other customers during a conflict — the 'denial' power, which companies fear could trigger breach-of-contract claims and scare off foreign buyers — and whether the Pentagon will indemnify partners against satellites damaged or destroyed in a conflict. Clayton Swope of CSIS's Aerospace Security Project noted that 'companies do not build extra capacity for sport,' and that it will be hard to entice firms to hold surge capacity at these dollar values and durations.
sections.whyItMatters: The concept — treat commercial space like the Civil Reserve Air Fleet — has been on paper since 2023 and is still being tested with seven-figure contracts. The unresolved denial and indemnification questions are the actual bottleneck; neither can be fixed with a contract award, and both require a policy decision the Pentagon has deferred.

sections.heading: Greenland Basing Moves to the Planning Cycle
sections.body:
The Pentagon is spending the winter evaluating options for expanding US basing in Greenland, with an eye toward breaking ground next year, a senior defense official told reporters at a Project on Media and National Security event, per Defense One. The official cited the weather execution window as the immediate constraint. Options under review include expanding the existing US footprint at Narsarsuaq in the south — including what runway upgrades would be needed to support modern US aircraft, from C-130s to fighters — and additional locations on the northeast and east coasts, with Mestersvig, which has a 6,000-foot gravel runway and has primarily hosted special operations forces, mentioned as an early candidate.

The official stressed the work is currently about feasibility — lodging, food, energy — rather than stationing specific capabilities. The planning follows the administration's broader push on Greenland, which began with a purchase proposal and escalated to threats against Denmark and other NATO allies before settling into a negotiated arrangement.
sections.whyItMatters: Arctic basing is infrastructure with a decade-long lead time, and once a runway is lengthened for fighters the capability exists whether or not a strategy document says so. For Denmark and NATO, the relevant fact is that US presence in Greenland is expanding under an arrangement negotiated after coercion — a durable alliance problem packaged as construction planning.

bottomLine: Today's developments were mostly industrial rather than dramatic: a corvette launch in Cádiz, a propulsion subcontract for Polish submarines, a training lease in Karlskrona, short-term space contracts worth under $2 million. That is where defense capability is actually decided. Poland's Orka program is now assembling a full supply and training chain toward 2031 deliveries, Japan has moved nuclear propulsion from taboo to a live planning question alongside Seoul and Canberra, and the US is building an autonomous-warfare command whose funding depends on a reconciliation bill that may not survive the new Congress in January. The pattern across all of it is that strategy documents are running ahead of the money, the workforce, and the price points that determine whether any of it reaches the field.
sources: Naval News, Breaking Defense, Defense One, Defense News, The War Zone (TWZ), South China Morning Post, SpaceNews, CSIS Aerospace Security Project, American Enterprise Institute, FMV / Royal Swedish Navy, Navantia, Hanwha Systems, Powerus, Heaviside
